newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa called to open little changed.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa called to open little changed.

text.p: CSCE cocoa futures were called to open little changed on Tuesday, on the heels of an uneventful performance in London overnight, traders said.
London cocoa futures softened in thin, rangebound trading early Tuesday. LIFFE July cocoa was off three stg at the midday break, to 1,021 stg, and September eased two stg, to 1,039 stg.
U.S. and London markets were both closed on Monday for holidays.

Friday, New York cocoa futures ended slightly lower in sluggish trading. July ended down $2 a tonne, at $1,461, after trading from $1,471 to $1,452. Second-month September also fell $2, to close at $1,491, while the back months sagged $2 to $6.

Technically, traders pegged July support at $1,450-$1,445. Near-term resistance was seen at $1,475, but traders said the spot contract would need to get past $1,490 and a chart gap between $1,498 and $1,501 to inspire substantial buying.

The latest CFTC Commitment of Traders report for the two weeks ended May 20 showed non-commercial long positions increased by 2,691 lots, to 13,594 lots. Non-commercial short positions decreased by 169 lots, to 5,001 lots.
Commercial long positions fell by 3,451 lots in the two weeks, to 64,562 lots, while commercial short positions fell by 95 lots, to 80,231 lots.
Nonreportable long positions rose by 1,349 lots, to 15,599 lots and nonreportable short positions rose by 853 lots, to 8,523 lots.

In other news, data released a conference by the Barry Callebaut group, a company formed by the merger of France's Cacao Barry and Swiss Callebaut ERG, showed it expects the world cocoa bean harvest to decline to 2.698 million tonnes in 1996/97 from 2.852 million tonnes in 1995/96, but to increase in the longer term.
Top producer Ivory Coast is expected to harvest 1.145 million tonnes of beans in 1996/97 against 1.151 million tonnes in the previous season, with higher production forecast for the longer term.
Barry Callebaut also expects world demand for cocoa beans to rise by three percent in 1996/97 to 2.76 million tonnes from 2.679 million in 1995/96.
